 GST on RMC job work for builders: Classification, rate change and key takeaways from Maharashtra AAR
 GST 22 Oct 2026 17 min read
 GST Treatment of RMC Job Work for Construction Sector: Analysis of In re Prayatna Infratech Pvt. Ltd. (GST AAR Maharashtra)
 1. Background and Context
 Ready-mix concrete (RMC) is widely used in large construction projects, and many developers set up on-site batching plants through third-party contractors. A recurring question under the GST regime is whether such arrangements amount to:
 Supply of goods (sale of RMC), or
 Supply of services (job work / processing services), and
 What is the correct Service Accounting Code (SAC) and GST rate , especially when the principal supplies all major inputs.
 The ruling in In re Prayatna Infratech Pvt. Ltd. (GST AAR Maharashtra) addresses these issues in detail, particularly the classification of RMC-related activities under Section 2(68) of the CGST Act, 2017 and the rate change effective from 22 September 2025 .
 This article explains the facts, reasoning and conclusions of the Authority for Advance Ruling (AAR), and distils compliance lessons for assessees engaged in similar RMC or outsourced manufacturing activities.
 2. Facts of the Case
 2.1 Parties and Business Arrangement
 Applicant : Prayatna Infratech Pvt. Ltd. , operating an automated RMC batching plant.
 Principal : Riverview City Constructions Limited (RCCL) , a registered person engaged in construction of residential and non-residential buildings.
 Key features of their arrangement:
 The RMC batching plant was installed and operated by the applicant at RCCL’s Riverview City project located at Loni Kalbhor, Pune .
 RCCL, being the project owner and a registered person, supplied the principal raw materials :
 Cement
 Sand
 Aggregates
 Water
 Admixtures
 These materials were supplied free of cost to the applicant.
 Ownership of both the raw materials and the finished RMC at all times vested with RCCL .
 The applicant provided:
 Plant and machinery
 Labour and supervision
 Process know-how and operational support
 The applicant incurred:
 Electricity charges
 Diesel and fuel costs
 Salaries and wages
 Repairs and maintenance expenditure
 2.2 Nature of Operations
 The activity carried out by the applicant consisted of:
 Receiving cement, sand, aggregates, water and admixtures belonging to RCCL.
 Undertaking precise:
 Weighing
 Batching
 Mixing
 Addition of chemicals and admixtures to required proportions
 Producing RMC tailored to RCCL’s technical specifications.
 Loading the RMC into transit mixers.
 Undertaking primary transportation of the RMC within RCCL’s construction site.
 Important factual points:
 The final product, RMC, was not supplied to any third party . It was exclusively used by RCCL in its own construction project.
 The invoices raised by the applicant were described as services relating to “Mixing and Primary Transportation of RMC” .
 The work orders clearly specified that the rates were “without material” , underscoring that the applicant was not selling RMC as goods.
 3. Questions Raised Before the AAR
 The applicant approached the Maharashtra AAR seeking clarity on:
 Classification of its activity under the appropriate Service Accounting Code (SAC) .
 Applicable GST rate :
 For the period up to and including 21 September 2025 ; and
 For the period from 22 September 2025 onwards , in light of the amendment to the rate notification.
 The applicant contended that:
 The process undertaken resulted in RMC, which is a commercially distinct commodity with its own name, character and use.
 This would qualify as “manufacture” within the meaning of Section 2(72) of the CGST Act, 2017 .
 At the same time, since the processing was carried out on goods belonging to a registered person (RCCL) , the activity should be regarded as:
 A supply of services in terms of paragraph 3 of Schedule II , and
 Job work as defined in Section 2(68) .
 4. Legal Framework Considered
 4.1 Statutory Provisions
 The AAR examined the following core provisions of the CGST Act, 2017 :
 Section 2(68) – Definition of job work :
 Any treatment or process undertaken by a person on goods belonging to another registered person.
 Section 2(72) – Definition of manufacture :
 Processing of raw materials or inputs in any manner that results in a new product having a distinct name, character and use.
 Paragraph 3 of Schedule II – Deeming fiction:
 Any treatment or process which is applied to another person’s goods is treated as a supply of services .
 4.2 Notifications and Circulars
 Key GST notifications and circulars analysed:
 Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28 June 2017 
Particularly, Serial No. 26(id) , governing job work services .
 Notification No. 15/2025-Central Tax (Rate), dated 17 September 2025 
Substituting Serial No. 26 and changing the rate structure from 22 September 2025 .
 Circular No. 237/71/96-CX, dated 12 August 1996 
(Central Excise) – relied on by the applicant to demonstrate that RMC is a manufactured, excisable product.
 Circular No. 38/12/2018-GST, dated 26 March 2018 
Clarifying that a job worker may use its own goods (like consumables, fuel, etc.) in addition to principal’s goods, without affecting job work status.
 Circular No. 126/45/2019-GST, dated 22 November 2019 
Distinguishing job work done on goods belonging to registered persons from residual “manufacturing services” on inputs of others .
 5. Positions of the Parties
 5.1 Applicant’s Submissions
 The applicant argued as follows:
 The transformation of cement, aggregates, sand and admixtures into RMC results in a new commercial product .
 RMC possesses an independent identity, and accordingly, the process fits the scope of manufacture under Section 2(72) .
 However, the goods always belong to another registered person (RCCL) . Therefore:
 The transaction is a supply of service under paragraph 3 of Schedule II (treatment or process applied to another’s goods).
 It satisfies the definition of job work in Section 2(68) .
